summary: This informational document clarifies terminology for Software-Defined Networking (SDN), an approach to running networks dynamically through open interfaces and software. It describes the layers and architecture commonly used to discuss SDN, so people use the same words for the same parts.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a road system controlled by one smart program instead of each traffic light thinking alone. This note names the parts of such a system so everyone talks about them the same way.

questions: what are the layers of sdn architecture
what is the difference between control plane and management plane
what is the network services abstraction layer
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the planes, abstraction layers and interfaces that make up a Software-Defined Network.

tldr.problem: People were confused about what exactly Software-Defined Networking is, which layers an SDN architecture has, and how those layers talk to each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines forwarding, operational, control, management and application planes, four abstraction layers (DAL, CAL, MAL, NSAL) and the interfaces between them, then maps technologies such as ForCES, NETCONF, OpenFlow, I2RS, SNMP, PCEP and BFD onto that picture.
tldr.outcome: It is a taxonomy from the IRTF SDN Research Group, not a standard. It gives the community common reference definitions without recommending any particular technology.

today: RFC 7426 is an Informational document from the IRTF, published in January 2015. The unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, and it is a taxonomy rather than a standard.

sections.title: What SDN Means and Why Define It
sections.content:
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is a programmable-networks approach in which software applications program individual network devices dynamically and so control the behaviour of the whole network. A key element is an abstraction between the forwarding and control planes that separates them, with the goal of reducing complexity and enabling faster innovation at both.

The RFC notes that definitions in the literature do not line up. For example, both OpenFlow and NETCONF have been called SDN interfaces, but they refer to control and management respectively. The document does not standardize any layer or interface and does not discuss the applicability of any framework. It is a taxonomy and a common base for discussion, reviewed by the IRTF SDN Research Group (SDNRG).
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone was using the word SDN to mean different things. This note is the dictionary.

sections.title: Core Terms
sections.content:
A resource is a physical or virtual component, from a port or queue up to a whole device. A network device performs packet manipulation and forwarding, and may be physical or virtual. An application is standalone software that uses services and offers no interfaces of its own, while a service provides APIs to applications or other services.

The planes are defined as:

  • Forwarding Plane (FP): the resources across all devices that forward traffic.
  • Operational Plane (OP): the resources that manage the operation of individual devices.
  • Control Plane (CP): the functions that control devices and instruct them how to process and forward packets.
  • Management Plane (MP): the functions that monitor, configure and maintain devices.
  • Application Plane: the applications and services that program network behaviour.

Four abstraction layers sit between them: DAL, CAL, MAL and NSAL.
sections.plainLanguage: There are parts that move the packets, parts that keep the box healthy, parts that decide where packets go, and parts that run the show.

sections.title: Planes, Layers and Interfaces
sections.content:
SDN rests on a controlled entity and a controller that manipulates it through an interface. Locally the interface is mostly API calls. It can be extended to a protocol, which may be open or proprietary and may run locally or remotely.

A network device lives in the forwarding plane (the data path) and the operational plane. Both are exposed through the Device and resource Abstraction Layer (DAL). The control plane reaches the DAL through the Control-Plane Southbound Interface (CPSI), via the Control Abstraction Layer (CAL). The management plane uses the Management-Plane Southbound Interface (MPSI) via the Management Abstraction Layer (MAL). Applications and services reach the control and management planes through the Network Services Abstraction Layer (NSAL), using service interfaces such as RESTful APIs or RPC.

The CPSI is time-critical and built for wire efficiency, with examples ForCES and OpenFlow. The MPSI is not time-critical and is closer to human interaction, with examples NETCONF, IPFIX, Syslog, OVSDB and SNMP. Control-plane peers talk over an east-west interface using protocols like BGP or PCEP.

The model is recursive: layers can be stacked and reused, and planes may be collocated or physically separated. Orchestration is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part talks to the one below it through a translator, so a planner does not have to know how every kind of box works inside.

sections.title: Control Versus Management
sections.content:
The RFC spends time on how the control and management planes differ, since the line blurs in SDN.

  • Timescale: the control plane sends updates often, roughly milliseconds, so it needs high bandwidth and low latency. The management plane acts over minutes, hours or even days.
  • Persistence: control-plane state such as routing is ephemeral. Management-plane state is persistent and survives reboots.
  • Locality: traditionally control is local and distributed while management is centralized and remote, but a logically centralized SDN controller muddles this.

The RFC also applies the CAP theorem (consistency, availability, partition tolerance; at most two at once). A centralized controller acts as a consistent global database, but when a switch cannot reach its controller the flow is unavailable until the connection returns. Multiple non-collocated controllers may improve partition tolerance at the cost of absolute consistency.
sections.plainLanguage: One part makes quick decisions all day, and another part makes slow decisions that stick around. When the planner is unreachable, the lights may just stop.

sections.title: Mapping Technologies onto the Model
sections.content:
The RFC argues the SDN southbound interface should include both CPSI and MPSI, and shows how prominent technologies fit.

  • ForCES models the forwarding plane with Logical Functional Blocks and offers simple Set, Get and Del commands. Its model suits the DAL and its protocol suits the CPSI.
  • NETCONF/YANG: YANG models configuration and state for the DAL and NETCONF suits the MPSI, but it was not originally designed for fast control-plane updates.
  • OpenFlow defines a DAL for the forwarding plane and a CPSI. The RFC describes version 1.4. OF-CONFIG uses NETCONF for the MPSI.
  • I2RS aims to make the Routing Information Base programmable and spans the control and application planes.
  • SNMP with MIBs describes the DAL and suits the MPSI.
  • PCEP serves path computation and is a control-plane service, usable east-west between PCEs.
  • BFD detects path failures and is usually an application on the device.
sections.plainLanguage: Every well-known tool gets filed under the right shelf, depending on whether it moves packets fast or manages the box slowly.

sections.title: Summary and Security
sections.content:
A network element is a composition of resources, each with a forwarding plane and an operational plane. The DAL abstracts them for services and applications in the control and management planes, and the NSAL exposes service abstractions to others. The taxonomy aims to establish commonly accepted reference definitions irrespective of implementation choices.

The RFC proposes no new architecture or protocol, so it says it has no impact on the security of the Internet. It still stresses that security is paramount and points to the literature and to the documents for each specific interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The note just draws the map and gives names. It does not build a new road, so it does not add new danger.
